papers.title: Validity and reliability of the Japanese version of the Movement Behaviour Questionnaire-Child (MBQ-C) for assessing active play, screen time, and sleep in preschool children
papers.abstract: Background: Valid and feasible measures of preschoolers' 24-hour movement behaviours are needed for population-level research. We developed a Japanese version of the Movement Behaviour Questionnaire-Child (MBQ-C) and evaluated its measurement properties and practicality. Methods: After translation and cross-cultural adaptation following the COSMIN procedure, including cognitive interviews, we evaluated the questionnaire in a cross-sectional validation study of Japanese children aged 3-6 years. Concurrent validity was assessed against hip-worn accelerometry and a 7-day diary; we also examined test-retest reliability, measurement error, agreement between response formats and modes, and practicality (completion time, burden, and clarity). Analyses used Spearman correlations, intraclass correlation coefficients, the SEM, smallest detectable change (SDC), and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. Results: Of 208 children, 170 provided valid accelerometer and diary data for the concurrent-validity analysis, and 187 completed the MBQ-C for the questionnaire-based analyses. Concurrent validity was weak for active and energetic play (Spearman {rho} = 0.12-0.26), strong for total screen time (0.78-0.85), and moderate for total sleep (0.48-0.58). Test-retest reliability was moderate to good (ICC, 0.66-0.81), and within-child variability was lowest for sleep (CV 3%) and highest for the physical activity items (21-33%). The open- and closed-ended versions showed no significant differences; paper-electronic agreement was good for screen time and sleep but poor for active play. Completion took approximately 6-9 minutes, with low reported burden. Findings were robust in sensitivity analyses. At the group level, SDC for a mean was SDCind/{surd}N: 119.8/{surd}N, 74.0/{surd}N, 112.6/{surd}N, and 92.5/{surd}N min/day for active play, energetic play, total screen time, and total sleep, respectively (N = number of children surveyed). The systematic differences between the two test-retest occasions were +15.7, +6.5, +4.0, and -5.4 min/day, respectively. Conclusions: The Japanese MBQ-C is a practical option for assessing preschoolers' active play, screen time, and sleep at the group level. By quantifying its group-level measurement error, this study provides benchmarks for interpreting group-level differences and change, supporting the use of the MBQ-C in surveillance and evaluation of programmes delivered at scale.

papers.title: A report-supervised EEG-language foundation model enables broad, interactive clinical interpretation
papers.abstract: Medical AI for complex signals such as electroencephalography (EEG) relies on costly expert annotations and predefined diagnostic labels that fail to capture the richness and nuance of clinical interpretation. Whether models trained on routine clinical reports can overcome these limitations while matching expert-supervised performance remains unclear. We introduce EEG Copilot, a biosignal-language foundation model trained on routine EEG-report pairs without dedicated task-specific expert annotations. Across two external datasets (6,078 EEGs), EEG Copilot performed on par with a state-of-the-art expert-supervised model across 11 shared findings (mean AUROC 0.80-0.81), corroborated by direct neurologist review of 200 EEGs. Beyond predefined diagnostic categories in conventional EEG AI, EEG Copilot assessed 23 clinical characteristics through natural-language questions in English and German across 9,689 EEGs from four hospitals (mean AUROC 0.80-0.82), demonstrating that automated EEG assessment need no longer be confined to fixed diagnostic outputs. Crucially, EEG Copilot generated integrated clinical impressions directly from EEG rather than isolated predictions with shuffled-report controls supporting recording-specific content and neurologist review of 800 impressions showing that most were accurate or clinically usable with minor errors. These findings chart a path beyond label-bound medical AI, transforming routine clinical reports into scalable supervision for flexible, language-driven assessment and integrated interpretation of complex physiological signals.

papers.title: Exploring the genetic determinants of ALS in a North Indian cohort using a genomic screening approach
papers.abstract: Background: Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis is a clinically and genetically heterogenous neurodegenerative disorder in which both monogenic and complex genetic mechanism contribute to disease susceptibility. Increasing evidence also indicates that non motor manifestations, including sleep disturbances, significantly influence disease burden. This study aimed to characterize the genetic spectrum of ALS in a predominantly North Indian cohort while evaluating the prevalence of sleep related abnormalities. Methods: Seventy-three clinically diagnosed ALS patients were recruited from a tertiary care centre in North India. Disease severity was assessed using the ALSFRS-R. Sleep quality, daytime sleepiness, and REM sleep behaviour disorder symptoms were evaluated using the PSQI, ESS and RBDQ questionnaires, respectively. Genetic analysis included targeted sequencing of SOD1, TARDBP, and ANG, followed by repeat expansion analysis of C9orf72, ATXN1, ATXN2, ATXN3, and ATXN7. Whole exome sequencing was performed in selected cases to further investigate the genetic basis of ALS. Results: The cohort demonstrated a male predominance and an earlier age of onset compared to many Western populations. Poor sleep quality and excessive daytime sleepiness were frequently observed although no significant association was found between sleep parameters and disease severity. Genetic screening identified a pathogenic/likely pathogenic TARDBP variant classified by ClinVar while no known or novel pathogenic variants were detected in SOD1 or ANG. Repeat expansion studies revealed one patient harbouring pathogenic C9orf72 repeat expansions. For the ATXN1, one patient harboured pathogenic repeat expansions and two patients carried intermediate length repeats. Additionally, one patient harboured intermediate repeat expansions in ATXN2. Whole exome sequencing revealed novel and rare variants in ALS associated genes including ANXA11, SIGMAR1, SETX, ERBB4 and NEK1, highlighting substantial genetic heterogeneity. Conclusions: Our findings highlight the complex genetic heterogeneity of ALS, with pathogenic repeat expansions and rare variants identified across multiple disease associated genes. These results demonstrate the importance of comprehensive genetic testing to improve the detection of clinically relevant variants in ALS. In addition, the high prevalence of sleep related disturbances observed in the cohort emphasizes the need to incorporate non motor assessment into routine clinical evaluation of patients with ALS.

papers.title: The ACROSSS-study. The role of sleep characteristics before and after a cardiovascular event. Rationale and study design.
papers.abstract: Studies of myocardial infarction and stroke showed a diurnal variation with peaks in the morning and afternoon. So far, night sleep or napping have not been investigated as triggers for cardiovascular events via a case-crossover study. Therefore, the main question of the ACROSSS (Acute CoROnary Syndrome, Stroke and Sleep) study is how much the occurrence of a myocardial infarction/stroke/transient ischemic attack is associated with taking a nap shortly before (topic 1, case-crossover study, 656 patients needed). Moreover, the study aims at assessing the incidence of sleep disturbances three and twelve months after a myocardial infarction/stroke/transient ischemic attack (topic 2, follow-up study, 400 patients needed). Recruitment of patients is carried out in four German hospitals in Essen and Bottrop, North Rhine-Westphalia. The examination program includes the case-crossover questionnaire on potential acute triggers of cardiovascular events, a sleep questionnaire with validated instruments (Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index, Epworth Sleepiness Scale, etc.) and a questionnaire on health status and lifestyle habits. Moreover, eligible patients are screened for sleep apnea and during the follow-up sleep is measured by actigraphy. The combination of sleep-related and clinical data offers a deeper understanding of how sleep affects the acute onset of a cardiovascular event and recovery afterwards.

papers.title: Targeting memory consolidation in major depression via pharmacological slow-wave sleep promotion
papers.abstract: Slow-wave sleep (SWS) has been implicated in memory consolidation and brain plasticity and proposed as a therapeutic target in major depressive disorder (MDD). However, whether pharmacological promotion of SWS causally improves memory consolidation remains unknown. Gamma-hydroxybutyrate (GHB), a robust enhancer of SWS, represents a promising drug-repurposing candidate to target this pathway. We therefore conducted a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial in 22 patients with MDD and 20 matched healthy controls receiving single nocturnal doses of GHB, trazodone as an active comparator, or placebo under polysomnographic monitoring (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT04082806). Declarative, procedural and emotional memory were assessed before and after sleep. GHB strongly increased SWS duration and delta power, whereas trazodone produced smaller changes in sleep-stage composition. Contrary to our hypothesis, neither drug improved memory consolidation across domains. Exploratory analyses revealed weak associations between global sleep-stage measures and memory, alongside selective associations with spindle and spectral features. These findings challenge the assumption that increasing SWS alone is sufficient to improve overnight memory consolidation and suggest that more targeted modulation of sleep oscillatory dynamics may be required.

papers.title: Motherly Plus: Study Protocol of a Randomized Controlled Trial Evaluating a Smartphone-Assisted Single-Session Psychotherapy Intervention for Postpartum Depression
papers.abstract: Introduction: Postpartum depression (PPD) is a public health problem, affecting approximately 17% of women worldwide. PPD is associated with significant costs to the healthcare system and impairments for the child. Although evidence shows that psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy are effective in reducing PPD symptoms, access to these treatments is limited, especially in low- and middle-income countries where there is a shortage of professionals and unequal distribution of mental health services. In this context, telehealth, smartphone apps, and brief psychotherapies emerge as viable, low-cost, and potentially scalable alternatives. However, gaps remain regarding the efficacy of single-session psychotherapies for PPD, especially when combined with digital support. Objectives: The primary objective is to test the efficacy of an intervention package combining single-session psychotherapy with subsequent self-guided use of a smartphone app for the treatment of PPD. Secondary objectives are to investigate moderators, mediators, and specific intervention processes. Method: A randomized clinical trial in which 104 women aged 18-40 years, up to 12 months postpartum, with a diagnosis of PPD will be randomized to the intervention (single-session psychotherapy supported by the Motherly app) or a waitlist. Participants in the intervention arm will retain access to the app throughout the study; waitlist participants will receive the intervention after post-treatment assessment. Assessments will occur at T1 (week 1, baseline), T2 (week 2, mid-treatment), T3 (week 4, post-treatment), and T4 (week 8, follow-up). The primary outcome will be depression assessed by the QIDS-C16 at T3. Secondary outcomes include anxiety, sleep, parental stress, and self-reported depression. Data will be analyzed using generalized estimating equations (GEE) models considering an intention-to-treat (ITT) perspective. Mediation models will be used to analyze mediators, while interaction models will be used to explore potential moderators. Regression models will be used to analyze the association between specific processes (therapeutic alliance and app engagement) and clinical outcomes. Perspectives: This study has potential public health relevance and innovation by testing an intervention package that combines single-session psychotherapy and technology, with high potential for scalability. Trial registration: clinicaltrials.gov NCT07925762 Key words: Postpartum depression; clinical trial; cognitive-behavior therapy; digital intervention; smartphone app; single session psychotherapy

papers.title: Impaired cortical gap-mediated inhibition in chronic tinnitus but with limited individual diagnostic accuracy
papers.abstract: Tinnitus lacks an objective marker, limiting diagnosis and treatment evaluation. We tested whether gap-mediated inhibition of cortical sound-evoked responses provides one. In a prospective, multicentre case-control study at seven sites in the United States and Europe, adults with and without chronic tinnitus heard brief pulses preceded or not by a silent gap, embedded in broadband or narrowband carriers, during electroencephalography. The primary outcome was inhibition of the N100 response. Of 584 eligible participants, 455 yielded high-quality recordings with complete covariate data (232 cases, 223 controls; mean age 45.4 years, 52% women) that entered the adjusted analyses. Inhibition was strongest for broadband noise whereas narrowband carriers gave limited dynamic range. Participants with tinnitus showed reduced broadband gap-mediated inhibition ({beta} = -19.27%, d = -0.413, cluster-corrected p = 0.002), scaling with tinnitus severity (covariate-adjusted {surd}THI model: partial R2 = 0.049, p = 0.0015). In contrast, discrimination of individuals was limited (AUC 0.612, 95% CI 0.560-0.663). Cortical gap inhibition is a reproducible group-level effect rather than an individual diagnostic test.

papers.title: Childhood sleep trajectories, hypomanic symptoms, and cognitive functioning in early adulthood: a longitudinal cohort study
papers.abstract: Background Sleep and circadian rhythm disturbances are implicated in bipolar disorder (BD), yet it remains unclear whether developmental trajectories of sleep and circadian rhythms across childhood confer risk for hypomanic symptoms (HS) and cognitive dysfunction. Here, we examined whether distinct sleep duration and sleep timing trajectories across childhood are associated with potential HS and cognitive functioning in early adulthood. Methods Using data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC), parent-reported night-time sleep duration and mid-point of sleep (MPS) from 6 months to 11 years were modelled using latent class growth analysis. During the ALSPAC study, HS were assessed at ages 21 to 23 using the Hypomania Checklist (HCL), and cognitive functioning (working memory and response inhibition) was assessed at age 24. Results Four sleep duration and three MPS trajectories were identified. Logistic regression analyses showed that persistently average shorter (OR=2.87, 95% CI=1.31 to 6.32) and persistently longer sleep (OR=2.81, 95% CI=1.08 to 7.30) trajectories were associated with increased risk of potential HS, while persistently earlier MPS was associated with lower odds (OR=0.23, 95% CI=0.11 to 0.49). Multiple linear regression models showed that experiencing HS in combination with persistently average shorter sleep was associated with poorer response inhibition (B=36.55, 95% CI=8.33 to 64.78, p=0.011), whereas HS in combination with persistently longer sleep was associated with better response inhibition (B=-125.21, 95% CI= -193.56 to -56.86, p<0.001). No interactions were found for working memory. Conclusions Persistently average shorter and persistently longer sleep duration trajectories were associated with increased risks of experiencing HS, as measured by the HCL, while earlier circadian timing were associated with reduced risks. Differences in early-life sleep regulation may be associated with subsequent risk of experiencing HS during early adulthood and may differentially shape subsequent response inhibition performance. Keywords: hypomania; sleep; trajectories; cognition; ALSPAC

papers.title: Altered oscillatory coupling and a candidate inhibitory circuit mechanism in Rett syndrome
papers.abstract: Rett syndrome (RTT) is a rare neurodevelopmental disorder caused primarily by pathogenic variants in the MECP2 gene and characterized by severe cognitive and neurological impairment. Phase amplitude coupling (PAC), a cross-frequency interaction supporting information integration across temporal and spatial scales, provides a window into large-scale neural coordination and circuit dysfunction. PAC depends on coordinated activity among specific neuronal subtypes, yet the cellular mechanisms shaping oscillatory dynamics in RTT remain poorly understood. Here we combined electroencephalography (EEG) with biophysically constrained computational modeling to characterize PAC alterations and investigate their circuit-level origins. Awake resting-state EEG was recorded from 42 individuals with RTT and 37 typically developing participants, and PAC strength was quantified. Individuals with RTT exhibited stronger PAC across widespread frequency pairs and cortical regions, including elevated theta gamma coupling in posterior, midline, and whole brain regions, and elevated alpha gamma coupling in anterior, posterior, and whole brain regions. Biophysically constrained network simulations of a cortical Layer 4 model comprising pyramidal neurons together with PV+, SOM+, and VIP+ interneurons demonstrated that reduced excitability of VIP+ interneurons selectively reproduced the increased theta gamma and alpha gamma PAC observed in RTT. These findings identify abnormal PAC as an electrophysiological feature of RTT and suggest a possible mechanistic link between altered oscillatory coordination and VIP+ interneuron dysfunction. PAC may provide a non-invasive marker of inhibitory circuit dysfunction and a translational framework for investigating shared circuit abnormalities across neurodevelopmental disorders.
